analysis.one_liner: Requires large electric suppliers to get a quarter of power from renewables and hit energy-saving targets.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 2013 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created two nationwide mandates on large energy suppliers. First, a federal renewable electricity standard: every large retail electric supplier would have to submit renewable energy credits covering 6% of its sales in 2015, rising to 25% for 2025 through 2040, with credits that can be traded and banked, and an option to pay $50 per missing credit into state renewable funds [S2][S3]. Second, a federal energy efficiency standard: large electricity and natural gas suppliers would have to achieve cumulative savings reaching 15% of electricity and 10% of gas sales by 2025, set at the maximum cost-effective level and verified annually [S2][S3]. States could run the program themselves, and the bill encouraged regulators to let utilities recover their costs and earn shareholder incentives for hitting efficiency targets [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses would benefit over time from mandated, cost-effective energy savings that lower electricity and gas use, plus reduced pollution from displaced fossil generation. Renewable energy developers gain a guaranteed national market through 2040, with bonus credits for rooftop solar, brownfield, and tribal-land projects.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every large retail electric supplier to submit renewable electricity credits equal to at least 6% of its sales in 2015, rising to 25% for 2025 through 2040.

Directs the Energy Department to set annual electricity and natural gas savings targets for large suppliers, reaching 15% cumulative electricity savings and 10% gas savings by 2025, set at the maximum achievable cost-effective efficiency level and never allowed to fall below the 2025 level.

Lets suppliers meet the targets by trading credits, banking them for three years, or buying verified savings from other suppliers, states, or third-party efficiency providers, and lets states take over administration of the efficiency program.

analysis.who_pays: Large electric and gas utilities bear compliance costs and penalties ($50 per missing renewable credit, doubled for violations; $100 per missing megawatt-hour of efficiency savings), which flow into customer rates; fossil-fuel generators lose sales share as renewables displace them.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs and penalties are recoverable through rates, so customers — including those least able to absorb increases — would bear much of the near-term cost, especially in regions dependent on fossil generation.

The bill directs regulators to let utilities recover lost margins from reduced sales and earn shareholder incentives when efficiency targets are met, locking in utility profits as a condition of the program rather than letting savings pass fully to customers.

Suppliers with no compliance history faced binding targets beginning in 2015, one year after expected enactment; the bill offered only a short delay of up to two years for the first reporting period, a steep ramp for some utilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The efficiency standard is designed to count only cost-effective savings, which should push energy bills down over time, and the renewable standard is market-based with trading and banking to find the cheapest clean power. The serious costs are near-term rate pressure in fossil-dependent regions and explicit protections for utility shareholder margins, which blunt how much of the efficiency benefit reaches customers. On balance a substantial public benefit, with real, acknowledged costs.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on October 31, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No senator joined as a cosponsor at any point in the bill's life.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote after the initial referral, and no further action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities and fossil-fuel generators never faced the federal renewable and efficiency mandates, and no compliance costs were imposed on ratepayers; renewable developers and efficiency providers lost the guaranteed national market the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities and fossil generators; renewable developers lost out

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — after the bill was referred, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors ever joined and no vote was ever recorded, so no partisan split appears in the record.

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers (wind, solar, geothermal, hydro)
industries.note: The bill creates a guaranteed national credit market through 2040, with bonus credits for rooftop and small distributed projects, brownfield sites, and generation on Indian land. Ordinary people share the benefit through cleaner air and, over time, cheaper clean power.

Their share of every large supplier's sales must shrink as the renewable percentage climbs, and $50-per-credit alternative compliance payments flow into state renewable and efficiency funds rather than back to them.

industries.industry: Large electric and natural gas utilities
industries.note: They face mandatory efficiency targets, annual reporting, and penalties of up to $100 per unsaved megawatt-hour, and efficiency cuts the sales they earn from. But the bill also encourages state regulators to let them recover lost margins and earn shareholder incentives for hitting efficiency targets, making utilities the paid channel for the program.
